snippet.title: Solar Quest Longplay (Arcade Version)
snippet.description:
- Solar Quest Longplay (Arcade Version) - 

Solar Quest is a multidirectional vector shooter designed and programmed by Scott Boden and released by Cinematronics in 1981. Its basic controls recall Asteroids, while the central sun brings to mind the gravitational hazards of the much earlier Spacewar! What gives it an identity of its own, however, is the decision to reward the player for rescuing the occupants of destroyed enemy spacecraft. Suddenly, shooting down an alien is only half the job.

Your ship is free to travel around the screen, using separate buttons to turn left, turn right and apply thrust. The usual momentum-based movement takes a little practice, particularly when trying to slow down near the sun. Anything that touches the star is destroyed, including enemy vessels and projectiles, and its gravitational influence becomes more pronounced as the game progresses.

The aliens initially wander around the battlefield before turning their attention to your ship. Early encounters are largely a matter of avoiding collisions, but later phases introduce enemies capable of firing back. Seven varieties of alien craft appear during each phase, and several kinds can occupy the screen at once. From the fifth phase onward, stronger gravity and the gradual introduction of enemy gunfire make the familiar surroundings considerably less forgiving.

Every ordinary enemy destroyed leaves behind a tiny survivor. Shooting this little figure earns 250 points, whereas flying over it to perform a rescue awards 1,000. Collecting enough survivors also earns an extra spacecraft, with the arcade operator able to set the requirement at either 25 or 40.

This is easily my favorite idea in the game. Flying away from a destroyed enemy would often be the sensible thing to do, but that little figure drifting toward the sun is awfully tempting. Rescuing it means abandoning a comfortable trajectory, adjusting your speed and possibly venturing into a part of the screen you would otherwise have avoided. The reward is generous enough to make the risk worthwhile, but not every rescue attempt is a good decision.

The ship also carries a limited supply of special projectiles that can eliminate several aliens in one blast. Unlike ordinary fire, these can be detonated manually with a second press of the corresponding button. Another is awarded at every 10,000-point interval. Hyperspace provides an escape from immediate danger, although relying on it too frequently temporarily disables the feature.

Then there are the Ghost Ships. These troublesome visitors appear if you go too long without destroying an alien, and they are capable of firing even in the early phases. They become increasingly persistent as the game advances. A Ghost Ship is worth 2,500 points, but leaves nobody behind to rescue. It is a clever way of discouraging a player from spending too much time simply circling the battlefield.

One aspect of the arcade original that deserves particular attention is the display. Cinematronics combined a monochrome vector monitor with a colored overlay, a reflective glass panel and a fluorescent backdrop illuminated by ultraviolet light. The result was an image that appeared to float in front of a field of stars. The monitor could also produce 64 brightness levels, an unusually sophisticated feature for a vector game of this period. A conventional gameplay recording cannot fully convey the visual effect of the original machine.

The Vectrex received its own conversion in 1982, but the coin-op remains especially interesting for the way its numbered phases gradually alter the balance of play. Familiar enemies become more dangerous, the sun becomes harder to escape and the time available for leisurely rescues shrinks. The escalating challenge continues until the player runs out of ships rather than leading to a conventional ending.

There is something wonderfully economical about this design. The battlefield hardly changes, yet the presence of a single drifting survivor can completely change your priorities. It is the sort of detail that makes a good vector shooter much more interesting than an exercise in aiming and firing. Solar Quest deserves considerably more recognition alongside the better-known space games of its generation.
